# About this course {.unnumbered}

How can we use computational models to learn something reliable about chemistry?

We begin with a familiar act of modelling: choosing what to retain and what to leave out. A molecular drawing, a calibration curve, and a neural network each represent selected aspects of a system. There is no final map of chemistry that serves every purpose. More detail may help with one question and obscure another. Our task is to notice the omissions and decide whether we can live with them for the question at hand.

Those choices are made by people. My starting point is that AI is a deeply human endeavour. People decide which questions are worth asking, what a system should learn, and what will count as a good answer. They produce the measurements, build the tools, and decide what to do with the results. When some of that work is automated, the choices have not gone away. Alongside learning to build and evaluate models, we will therefore examine the resources, labour, data choices, and institutional dependencies of our research tools.

We approach AI as an ambition: building systems with capabilities we associate with intelligence. That ambition is too broad to specify a technical question. Throughout the course, we ask which task a system performs, how it works, under which conditions it will be used, and what evidence supports its claims.

Many of the ambitions behind today's systems have a long history. DENDRAL was already tackling chemical structure elucidation in the 1960s; we will meet it alongside more recent applications below. We will also examine how scientific results enter commercial claims about models. A result can advance research and help sell a product at the same time. To distinguish an achievement from the promise surrounding it, we need to follow the claim back to what was actually tested. The [opening lecture](lectures/01-ai-and-science.qmd#science-and-model-claims) works through one such example.

To make the modelling choices easier to discuss, we will use three contrasts: **correlative versus causal, Bayesian versus frequentist, and connectionist versus symbolic**. Are we finding patterns for prediction or asking what happens when we intervene? What do we mean by probability? How is knowledge represented and used? These questions concern different choices, and a system can combine approaches. Even after choosing an approach, we still have to decide what the model should learn. Calling a molecule “soluble,” for example, hides a decision about how much solubility is enough. Throughout the course, we will ask whether the lenses fit the problem and whether we have gathered the evidence our conclusion needs.

This course follows our opening question through what might seem like a collection of buzzwords: statistical learning, molecular representations, deep learning, molecular simulation, generative models, and experimental design. We will make these terms concrete by building models, inspecting their failures, and asking what their results support scientifically.

## How we will work {#how-to-use-a-lecture-page}

These notes are for master's students in chemistry. We develop the Python and machine-learning ideas alongside the chemical problems, starting with small examples. The first meeting introduces the course questions, helps you set up the tools, and includes a discussion of the timetable.

We will spend time with small examples: a molecular drawing, a few measurements, a line that does not quite fit. They give us something to work out together, on the board or on paper, before we ask a program to do the calculation. These notes develop the same arguments in more detail, so you can return to them afterwards.

Later, more of that work will happen in Python notebooks. Some preparation will help us start the practicals, but we will learn how the methods work together in class. We will also use large language models for help with code and explanations. That gives us another model to question: did its suggestion help, and how do we know?

The [glossary](glossary.qmd) explains technical terms with examples from chemistry and our computing tools. Linked terms in the notes take you directly to the relevant entry.

Several books have shaped how I think about these questions. I particularly recommend Hardt and Recht's *Patterns, Predictions, and Actions*, Kate Crawford's *Atlas of AI*, Carissa Véliz's *Prophecy*, and Simon J. D. Prince's *Understanding Deep Learning*. I have collected them with the papers discussed in class under [suggested reading](reading.qmd). The reading is optional.

## Different ways of doing chemistry {#examples-through-lenses}

“AI in chemistry” can mean proposing a molecular structure, choosing an experiment, or checking the steps of a theoretical derivation. These involve quite different ways of working with knowledge. A few examples make the breadth of the term apparent.

First, a few examples of what researchers have actually done. The tabs below return to them through the three contrasts. Some distinctions matter more for one example than another; a proof checker, for instance, need not attach a probability to the derivation it checks.

| Example | What was the scientific task? |
|---|---|
| [DENDRAL — Duffield et al. (1969)](https://doi.org/10.1021/ja01039a026) | Propose molecular structures consistent with a formula and mass spectrum; this study examined ketones. |
| [Lean in chemical physics — Bobbin et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1039/D3DD00077J) | Formalise derivations in adsorption theory and relationships between gas laws. |
| [ANI-1 — Smith et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1039/C6SC05720A) | Estimate molecular energies from atomic identities and positions using a learned approximation to reference calculations. |
| [Retrosynthesis — Segler et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature25978) | Find possible routes from a target molecule back to available starting materials. |
| [Antibacterial screening — Stokes et al. (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2020.01.021) | Prioritise compounds for experimental testing, leading to the identification of antibacterial activity in halicin. |
| [Molecular generation — Gómez-Bombarelli et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1021/acscentsci.7b00572) | Generate molecular candidates and search for desirable properties in a learned continuous representation. |
| [A mobile robotic chemist — Burger et al. (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2) | Choose and perform experiments to improve photocatalytic hydrogen production. |
| [AlphaFold2 — Jumper et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2) | Predict three-dimensional protein structures from sequence and associated information. |
| [ChemCrow — Bran et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-024-00832-8) | Coordinate software tools for chemical tasks, including synthesis planning and execution on a connected platform. |

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Correlative / causal

Suppose a model finds a reliable association between molecular structure and an experimental outcome. We can use it to predict another outcome. To ask what would happen if we changed something in the experiment, we need to consider how that change relates to the observations. This is the distinction between correlative prediction and causal modelling. Explaining the fitted model's calculation leaves the intervention question open.

| Example | What becomes visible through this distinction? |
|---|---|
| Antibacterial screening | A learned association helps select compounds. Follow-up experiments supply evidence about their activity under the tested conditions. Establishing the biological mechanism asks for further evidence. |
| AlphaFold2 | Predicting a structure and predicting the effect of a particular intervention are different tasks. Agreement with measured structures alone does not establish a causal account of protein function. |
| ANI-1 | Agreement with reference energies tests a learned approximation. Using it to study a changed molecule or a trajectory also requires a justified physical model and evidence that the approximation works there. A learned component can sit inside a physically motivated simulation. |
| A mobile robotic chemist | The robot changes experimental conditions and measures outcomes. An optimisation result shows what worked in the explored space; identifying the effect of an individual component requires an appropriate comparison. |
| Lean in chemical physics | A proof establishes what follows from specified premises. Whether those premises describe a physical intervention remains a question about the experiment and the theory being formalised. |

The [reaction example](lectures/01-ai-and-science.qmd#what-changes-when-the-task-is-science) develops the distinction slowly. A causal model can also make predictions; the question here is what supports an intervention claim.

### Bayesian / frequentist

Suppose we attach a probability to a result. What does that number describe? Bayesian inference represents uncertainty through a probability model, including a prior, and updates it with observations. Frequentist inference studies the behaviour of procedures under repeated sampling. Both require modelling assumptions. The [probability reading](reading.qmd#probability-lenses) gives a short introduction.

| Example | What would we ask about probability and uncertainty? |
|---|---|
| A mobile robotic chemist | The study uses a Bayesian search algorithm. What assumptions shape its uncertainty and its next experimental choice? We could separately ask how often the whole procedure succeeds over repeated runs. The inferential approach and the evaluation question need not belong to one exclusive camp. |
| ANI-1 and AlphaFold2 | Calling a model a neural network does not tell us whether its uncertainty is treated in a Bayesian or frequentist way. For any reported confidence or error measure, we need to inspect how it was constructed and what it is intended to mean. |
| Lean in chemical physics | Checking a derivation is a logical task. A probability interpretation becomes relevant if we also model uncertainty in measurements or premises; it is not supplied by the proof checker itself. |

We will return to this lens when uncertainty becomes useful for deciding what to measure next. For now, “the model is confident” is an invitation to ask how that confidence was defined.

### Connectionist / symbolic

How does useful knowledge enter the system? A symbolic approach works with explicit representations, rules, and operations. A connectionist approach learns distributed representations in networks of interacting units. We can also combine them, as several of these examples do.

| Example | Where does the useful knowledge or capability come from? |
|---|---|
| DENDRAL | Explicit chemical rules constrain a search over candidate structures and their compatibility with spectral data. |
| Lean in chemical physics | Researchers express definitions, assumptions, and proofs formally; Lean checks the derivations using its logical foundations and mathematical library. |
| ANI-1 | Neural networks learn from calculated energies, using [representations](glossary.qmd#representation) of local atomic environments. |
| Retrosynthesis | Neural networks guide a tree search over possible reaction steps. Learned preferences and symbolic search work together. |
| Antibacterial screening | A neural model learns from molecular structures and measured growth inhibition; researchers select and test candidates. |
| Molecular generation | An [encoder and decoder](glossary.qmd#generative-model) learn a continuous molecular representation; optimisation searches that space for candidates with desired scores. |
| A mobile robotic chemist | Bayesian optimisation selects experiments; robotic equipment executes them. Automation alone tells us little about whether a system uses neural representations or explicit rules. We need to inspect its components. |
| AlphaFold2 | Neural networks combine learned structural patterns with sequence, evolutionary, and structural information. |
| ChemCrow | An LLM selects and calls specialised tools, then uses their outputs to continue the task. The tools supply additional capabilities and information. |

:::

### What do we ask the model to learn? {#choices-within-a-lens}

Suppose we want to choose molecules for an experiment that requires a dissolved concentration of 1 mmol/L. We decide to learn from measured solubilities under the conditions of that experiment. The broad approach is correlative modelling. But what, exactly, should the model predict?

For a small example, suppose three molecules, A, B, and C, have measured solubilities of 0.2, 2, and 20 mmol/L under those same conditions. We could keep these values, turn them into labels, or retain only their order. These give us three possible learning tasks:

| What we ask the model to predict | What happens to the information in our example? |
|---|---|
| **The solubility value** — [regression](glossary.qmd#regression) | We retain 0.2, 2, and 20 mmol/L. The values let us compare different concentration requirements; we still have to decide which requirement matters. |
| **Whether it is soluble enough for this experiment** — [classification](glossary.qmd#classification) | We turn the values into “no, yes, yes.” B and C receive the same label even though their solubilities differ tenfold. The 1 mmol/L requirement has become part of what we ask the model to learn. |
| **The order of the candidates by solubility** — [ranking](glossary.qmd#ranking) | We retain C before B before A. The order would be identical if every solubility were a hundred times lower, although none of the molecules would then meet our requirement. |

Now suppose the next experiment requires 5 mmol/L. If we kept only the old yes/no labels, we cannot tell that B no longer qualifies while C does. The information disappeared when we made the labels. A more elaborate model trained on those labels does not restore the missing measurements. The choice that looked like a matter of format has changed which questions the data can answer.

Even if we keep numerical values, we still have to decide what counts as a large mistake. Predicting 0.1 instead of 0.01 mmol/L and predicting 10 instead of 1 mmol/L are both tenfold overestimates. Their absolute errors are 0.09 and 9 mmol/L. A [loss](glossary.qmd#loss) based on absolute differences makes the second error a hundred times larger; one based on differences between logarithms treats them equally. Which comparison serves our experiment? Choosing a scale has already expressed a preference about the mistakes we care about. In the [calibration example](lectures/02-learning-from-data.qmd#which-model-is-better), we will see two error measures favour different models on the same observations.

This is what I mean by further choices within a lens. We have stayed with the same broad approach, yet changed what is retained, what counts as an answer, and what is rewarded during learning. These decisions deserve to be argued for as carefully as the choice of method.

Consider one of the research examples through two of these lenses. What becomes visible through each? What do we still need to know? The [original studies](reading.qmd#application-examples) describe the choices their authors made.

## Beginning with a straight line {#our-first-hands-on-example}

We begin with a calibration curve and a small set of generated observations. Even fitting a straight line gives us decisions to make: which information to use, which errors to care about, and where we expect the result to work. We can examine those decisions with a little algebra before writing much code.
